translations.text: As the wise Solomon says in Ecclesiastes, "it abides forever", and it serves all generations and nourishes each of those who come upon it in turn.
But men, who have no authority even over their own selves, but are subject to the will of the One who holds them, when they do not know it,
enter into this life, and again, when they do not wish it, they depart from it. Yet out of their great vanity they
think that they are lords of this ever-standing world, they who are born and die from one time to another.
But the one who understands all this, and for this reason holds in contempt every affair of the world
that men esteem as honorable, and has love only for that divine life, the one who knows that:
"All flesh is grass, and all the glory of man is as the flower of grass", how could such a one ever count as desirable the "grass" that is here today and tomorrow becomes nothing?
For the one who truly understands knows that not only do human affairs have no firmness, but neither does the whole world abide without end.
For this reason he regards the life of this transient world as foreign to him and passing away.
For according to the word of the Savior, "heaven and earth will pass away", and all material things will be changed. And for this reason, as long as such a person is still "in this flesh",
this vain life seems heavy to him, and he laments that this sojourn is prolonged, as the Psalmist does in his songs.
For truly "those who have become sojourners" are in darkness among these evils.
For this reason the prophet sighed over the prolonging of his sojourn and said:
"Woe is me, for my sojourn has been prolonged." And he gave that dwelling the name "darkness" and said:
"And I dwelt with those who dwell in Kedar", for in the Hebrew language "darkness" is called "Kedar", as we have learned from the wise. Or is it not so?
Truly, men are as blind as if they were held fast by deep darkness, so that they cannot recognize the deception of the world. They do not know
that whatever men in this life count as good or evil is so only in the opinion of the senseless.
For in themselves these things are nothing. Being a child of the poor is nothing, and being a child of the rich is nothing; glory and wealth are nothing,
and so are strength, poverty and weakness. Authority over others is nothing, and so are slavery and every other inequality of this world.
But in the eyes of the foolish there is a great difference between these things, for they make carnal desire the judge of such matters.
But the one whose mind has reached the divine height sees all these things as equal, and none of these matters seems to him in any way more honorable than another, because
in rest and in affliction, in wealth and in poverty,
in slavery and in lordship, the race of our life is run in the same way, and both have the same power to bring us to the end,
whether the life is good or evil, as the apostle says: "with weapons on the right hand and on the left, through glory and dishonor."
For in both of these kinds of life the person who understands and is watchful walks his road in the same way and hurries to reach his end,
